questions.question: What are the different states in the EC2 instance lifecycle?
questions.answer: EC2 instances pass through these states: Pending (booting, no charge), Running (active, compute charged), Stopping (transition), Stopped (off, only EBS charged), Rebooting (restart on same host), Hibernating (RAM saved to EBS, only EBS charged), Shutting-down (transition to delete), and Terminated (permanently deleted, no charges).

questions.question: In which EC2 instance state does AWS charge for compute?
questions.answer: AWS charges EC2 compute costs only in the Running state. All other states — Pending, Stopping, Stopped, Rebooting, Hibernating, Shutting-down, and Terminated — do not incur compute charges. However, EBS storage is charged whenever the volume is provisioned (Running, Stopped, Hibernating).

questions.question: What is vertical scaling? Give an example.
questions.answer: Vertical scaling means changing the resources of a single existing instance — increasing (scale up) or decreasing (scale down) its CPU and RAM by changing the instance type. Example: upgrading a T3.micro (2 vCPU, 1 GB RAM) to a T3.large (2 vCPU, 8 GB RAM) because your application needs more memory.

questions.question: What is horizontal scaling? How is it different from vertical scaling?
questions.answer: Horizontal scaling means adding (scale out) or removing (scale in) instances to distribute load. Example: going from 1 to 3 EC2 instances behind a load balancer. Unlike vertical scaling, horizontal scaling does not require stopping existing instances, so there is no downtime. Vertical scaling makes one server bigger; horizontal scaling adds more servers.

questions.question: What is Termination Protection and when should you use it?
questions.answer: Termination Protection is an EC2 setting that prevents an instance from being terminated until the protection is explicitly disabled. Once enabled, any attempt to terminate the instance — from the console, CLI, or automation — will fail with an error. Enable it on any production server, database instance, or critical resource where accidental deletion would cause a significant incident.

questions.question: What is Shutdown Behavior in EC2 and what are the options?
questions.answer: Shutdown Behavior determines what happens to an EC2 instance when the OS-level shutdown command is executed from within the virtual machine (e.g., sudo shutdown now on Linux or Shut Down from Windows Start menu). There are two options: Stop (default) — the instance enters the Stopped state and can be restarted; Terminate — the instance is permanently deleted.

questions.question: What is EC2 Hibernation and how does it differ from stopping?
questions.answer: Hibernation saves the entire RAM contents (memory dump) to the EBS root volume, then pauses the instance. When started again, the OS restores the RAM from EBS and resumes exactly from the paused state — all applications continue mid-execution. In contrast, stopping clears RAM entirely, so applications must restart from scratch on next boot. Both charge only for EBS storage (not compute) while paused.

questions.question: Does AWS charge for EBS when an EC2 instance is stopped?
questions.answer: Yes. EBS storage is charged whenever the volume is provisioned and allocated — regardless of whether the instance is running, stopped, or hibernating. AWS only stops all charges when the instance is terminated (which also deletes the root EBS volume by default).

questions.question: What are the three dimensions AWS charges for when using EC2?
questions.answer: AWS charges for: (1) Compute — per second or hour based on instance type and OS, only while running. (2) EBS Storage — per GB-month provisioned, charged in all states except terminated. (3) Data Transfer Out — charged for data leaving the AWS network to the internet; data transfer in is free.

questions.question: What is the difference between scale-out and scale-up?
questions.answer: Scale-up is vertical scaling — making an existing instance larger (more CPU/RAM) by changing its instance type. Scale-out is horizontal scaling — adding more instances to the fleet. Scale-up requires stopping the instance (downtime); scale-out can happen while existing instances continue running (no downtime for existing workloads).

questions.question: Walk me through how you would resize a production EC2 instance with minimal disruption.
questions.answer: (Situation) A production web server's T3.medium CPU was consistently at 90%, causing slow response times. (Task) Needed to upgrade to T3.large with zero user-visible downtime. (Action) I used a Blue-Green approach: launched a new T3.large instance from the same AMI, deployed the application, ran smoke tests, then shifted load balancer traffic to the new instance while keeping the old one running. Once verified, I terminated the old instance. (Result) Zero downtime, no customer impact, upgrade completed in 20 minutes.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to recover from or prevent accidental resource deletion in AWS.
questions.answer: (Situation) A teammate had full EC2 access and accidentally terminated a dev instance with 3 weeks of configuration work. (Task) Needed to prevent this from happening again. (Action) I immediately enabled Termination Protection on all shared instances. I also reviewed IAM policies and implemented least-privilege — developers got permissions to stop/start but not terminate. I set up automated AMI snapshots so that even if termination happened, we could recover quickly. (Result) No further accidental deletions. The team also adopted tagging to identify instance criticality.

questions.question: Describe a scenario where you would recommend horizontal scaling over vertical scaling.
questions.answer: (Situation) An e-commerce platform anticipated a 10x traffic spike during a sale event. (Task) Needed to handle the spike without single points of failure. (Action) Rather than resizing one large instance (which has a ceiling and requires downtime), I recommended setting up an Auto Scaling Group with a minimum of 2 instances and a maximum of 10 behind an Application Load Balancer. This way, instances scale out automatically as traffic grows and scale in as it reduces. (Result) The platform handled the spike with zero downtime, and costs returned to baseline automatically after the event.

questions.question: How would you handle an unexpected AWS bill as a beginner student?
questions.answer: (Situation) A student accidentally left an EC2 instance running over a weekend and received an unexpected $15 bill. (Task) Needed to address the charge without paying it immediately. (Action) Contact AWS Support via the console, open a billing support case, explain honestly that you are a student in cloud training who was unaware that resources were still running. AWS has a history of granting one-time credit for genuine student mistakes. Meanwhile, immediately terminate the instance and enable billing alerts to prevent future incidents. (Result) AWS typically waives the charge on first occurrence for students.

questions.question: Describe the stop-start IP address behavior and how you would handle it in production.
questions.answer: (Situation) A web application's DNS was pointing to the EC2 public IP. After a scheduled maintenance stop-start, the IP changed and the site went down. (Task) Needed to ensure consistent connectivity regardless of stop-start cycles. (Action) Allocated an Elastic IP address (static public IP), associated it with the instance, and updated the DNS record to point to the Elastic IP. Also documented this in the runbook. (Result) Subsequent stop-starts no longer changed the public-facing address. Important note: Elastic IPs are free when associated with a running instance but incur a small charge when unassociated.

questions.question: Walk me through what happens at the hardware level when you change an EC2 instance type.
questions.answer: (Situation) A developer asked me to explain why changing instance types requires a stop. (Task) Needed to explain the underlying hardware behavior. (Action) I explained: AWS data centers have physical host machines with CPU, RAM, and separate EBS storage racks, all connected via a hypervisor. Your EC2 is a virtualized slice of that host. Your EBS volume is a separate block from the storage rack, connected to your virtual machine. When you change instance type, AWS detaches the CPU and RAM allocation from the old virtual hardware configuration and reattaches a new allocation — T3.micro gets 2 vCPU + 1 GB RAM, T3.large gets 2 vCPU + 8 GB RAM. Your EBS data stays intact throughout because it is a separate device. The stop is needed to safely detach and reattach the virtual compute configuration.

questions.question: A developer SSH'd into a production EC2 and ran sudo shutdown now. The instance stopped and the application went down. What configurations would have prevented this?
questions.answer: (Situation) OS-level shutdown stopped a production server unintentionally. (Task) Identify preventive configurations. (Action) Two settings would prevent this: First, Stop Protection — if enabled, the stop action is blocked even when triggered from inside the OS via shutdown behavior. The instance remains running. Second, Shutdown Behavior change — if set to Stop (default) but Stop Protection is enabled, the OS shutdown cannot complete the stop. Alternatively, set Shutdown Behavior to Terminate combined with Termination Protection — both actions are blocked. (Result) The instance would remain running, and the developers would need to disable the protection explicitly before any shutdown.

questions.question: Explain the conflict between Termination Protection and Shutdown Behavior set to Terminate.
questions.answer: (Situation) A teammate configured Shutdown Behavior to Terminate for automated cleanup, but Termination Protection was already enabled. They ran sudo shutdown from inside the OS expecting the instance to be deleted. (Task) Explain what happened and why. (Action) When Shutdown Behavior is Terminate, an OS-level shutdown instructs AWS to delete the instance. However, Termination Protection is a higher-priority safeguard — it blocks all termination requests, regardless of source. So when the shutdown ran, AWS checked the Termination Protection flag, found it enabled, and kept the instance running. (Result) The instance remained running. This is by design — Protection settings always take the upper hand over Shutdown Behavior.

questions.question: When would you use hibernation instead of stopping an EC2 instance?
questions.answer: (Situation) A data scientist ran a complex ML preprocessing job that took 4 hours to reach a checkpoint. They needed to pause for the day without losing the in-memory state. (Task) Identify the best pause strategy. (Action) Recommended hibernation over stop: stopping would clear RAM, requiring the 4-hour process to restart from scratch. Hibernation saves the RAM dump to EBS, so on restart the preprocessing resumes from the exact checkpoint. Confirmed the instance met hibernation prerequisites: Nitro-compatible, encrypted EBS root volume with sufficient free space for the RAM dump. (Result) The scientist hibernated the instance, and the next morning it resumed mid-process within seconds.

questions.question: Your manager asks why your dev team's AWS bill increased this month even though the team stopped all instances over the weekend. Explain.
questions.answer: (Situation) EC2 instances were stopped over the weekend but EBS charges still appeared on the bill. (Task) Explain the billing behavior to the manager. (Action) Stopped EC2 instances still incur EBS storage charges because the volumes remain allocated and attached. AWS charges per GB-month for provisioned EBS storage — regardless of whether the instance is running. Additionally, check for Elastic IPs that are not associated with running instances (these also incur charges). To completely eliminate all charges, instances must be terminated, not just stopped. (Result) The manager understood the difference between stopping (pauses compute only) and terminating (stops all charges but deletes data).

questions.question: How does EC2 pricing vary and what factors should you consider when selecting a region for a workload?
questions.answer: EC2 pricing varies across three dimensions: instance type (larger = more expensive), operating system (Windows costs more than Linux due to licensing), and AWS region. US-East-1 (N. Virginia) is typically the cheapest region. Asia Pacific regions like Mumbai or Singapore cost 10–20% more. For most applications, the correct region choice is driven by latency to end users, not cost — but for batch processing jobs with no latency sensitivity, choosing the cheapest region makes financial sense. Always validate current prices using the AWS Pricing Calculator.

questions.question: What is the AWS Nitro System and how does it relate to EC2 instance resizing?
questions.answer: The AWS Nitro System is AWS's modern hypervisor and virtualization platform that offloads network, storage, and security functions to dedicated purpose-built hardware. This improves EC2 performance by freeing the host CPU from virtualization overhead. For resizing, Nitro enables live resizing (hot change) — modifying CPU and memory without stopping the instance — for supported configurations within the same instance family. Cross-family changes (e.g., T3 to C5) still require a stop. Most modern instance families (T3, M5, C5, R5, and newer) run on Nitro infrastructure.

questions.question: Explain the full architecture of what happens when you launch a T3.micro EC2 instance.
questions.answer: When you request a T3.micro: (1) AWS selects an available physical host in your chosen Availability Zone that has capacity. (2) The Nitro hypervisor allocates 2 virtual CPUs and 1 GB RAM from the host's physical pool. (3) AWS connects an EBS volume from the storage rack to your virtual machine via the Nitro network interface. (4) The Amazon Machine Image (AMI) is used to initialize the operating system on that EBS volume. (5) Security Groups are attached as virtual firewall rules at the hypervisor layer. (6) A public IP is assigned from AWS's IP pool. (7) The instance enters Pending state as the OS boots, then transitions to Running when all checks pass.

questions.question: How would you architect a zero-downtime vertical scaling approach for a production database on EC2?
questions.answer: True zero-downtime vertical scaling for a standalone database is difficult because databases often cannot be easily replicated mid-transaction. Best approach: (1) Set up database replication first — promote a read replica or create a standby instance. (2) Redirect application writes to the standby while the primary is being resized. (3) Stop the primary, change instance type, restart. (4) Verify replica-primary sync, then fail back to the primary. (5) Alternatively, use AWS RDS instead of EC2 for managed databases — RDS supports multi-AZ deployments where failover during instance class changes is nearly seamless. This is why production databases should use RDS rather than self-managed EC2 whenever possible.

questions.question: A company needs to reduce AWS costs on 20 EC2 instances used for batch processing that run 8 hours per weekday. What EC2 management practices would you recommend?
questions.answer: For batch workloads running predictable hours: (1) Stop all instances when batch jobs complete — do not leave them running 24/7. This alone saves 66% of compute costs (16 idle hours out of 24 not charged). (2) Evaluate Scheduled Auto Scaling — automatically start instances at 8 AM weekdays and stop at 6 PM. (3) For even more savings, use Spot Instances for fault-tolerant batch workloads — up to 90% cheaper than On-Demand. (4) Right-size instances using CloudWatch metrics — if CPU averages 30%, consider a smaller type. (5) Set up AWS Budgets alerts so unexpected resource overruns are detected immediately. (6) Enable Delete on Termination for EBS on non-persistent workloads to avoid orphaned storage charges.
